---
title: "Declarative Macros with `macro_rules!`"
description: "One Rust language concept taught with one short runnable example and a precise explanation."
---

## The question

**Why does `println!` have an exclamation mark?**

`println!` is a macro invocation. Unlike an ordinary function, a macro can accept token patterns and expand into Rust syntax **at compile time**. The simplest user-defined form is `macro_rules!`.

## The rule to remember

Macros generate syntax. Prefer ordinary functions when a function can express the same operation clearly.

## The smallest complete example

Paste into `main.rs` and run with `rustc --edition 2024 main.rs && ./main`. The [Rust examples page](examples/index.qmd) describes how to check all snippets automatically.

~~~rust
macro_rules! twice {
    ($x:expr) => { $x + $x };
}
fn main() {
    let n = 3;
    println!("{}", twice!(n)); // 6
}
~~~

**Follow the state:** `$x:expr` accepts an expression token fragment. Calling `twice!(n)` expands to an expression equivalent to `n + n`, producing 6. The expansion is checked as Rust code.

## Important limitation

This macro evaluates `$x` twice. For `twice!({ counter += 1; counter })`, side effects happen twice; an ordinary `fn twice(x: i32) -> i32 { x + x }` is safer for simple arithmetic. Use macros only when you actually need syntax generation.
